title: Treatment Planning
subtitle: Define outcomes before training starts
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating treatment planning within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain treatment planning without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in treatment planning.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to treatment planning.

sections.explainSimply: Treatment planning states what change would matter in daily life and how it will be measured.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Use baseline symptom and functional measures, concurrent-treatment documentation, expected dose, review intervals and stopping rules.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Plans should distinguish proximal outcomes (signal learning), intermediate outcomes (task performance) and distal outcomes (function and wellbeing).
sections.thinkOfItLike: A rehabilitation plan: define the target, dose, measurement and stopping rule before changing the exercise.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand treatment planning to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Without predefined outcomes, normal fluctuation can be mistaken for success.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using treatment planning predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Without predefined outcomes, normal fluctuation can be mistaken for success. Evidence classification: established clinical practice.

quizBank.question: How should the evidence for Treatment Planning be communicated?
